html:
Harsha was the emperor who ruled much of north India from 606 to 647, first as king of Thanesar and then from his capital at Kannauj. He was the last ruler to hold the north together before it broke into rival kingdoms.

He came to the throne young, after his elder brother was murdered, and spent his early reign at war. At his height his realm stretched across the Ganges plain, with the Narmada River as its southern edge. When he pushed south, the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II beat him on the Narmada and held the Deccan for the Chalukyas.

Harsha is unusually well known for a king of this age, thanks to two writers:

  • The court poet Banabhatta wrote the Harshacharita, a life of the king.
  • The Chinese monk Xuanzang stayed at his court and praised his justice and his gifts to monks.

He backed Buddhist learning at Nalanda while also honouring Hindu gods, and he wrote three Sanskrit plays himself. He died without an heir. The struggle for Kannauj that followed drew in the Palas, the Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas for two centuries.
